key_terms.meaning: The point where the whole area of a section may be taken to act; for a section it is at x̄ = Σaᵢxᵢ/Σaᵢ, ȳ = Σaᵢyᵢ/Σaᵢ, with areas aᵢ in mm² and distances in mm.
I = Σaᵢyᵢ² about an axis, in mm⁴; it measures how spread out the area is from that axis and so how stiff the section is in bending.
I_axis = I_centroid + A d², where A is the area (mm²) and d the distance between the two parallel axes (mm).
The line in the cross-section where bending stress is zero; it passes through the centroid of the section.
A cross-section that is plane before bending stays plane after bending — this is what makes strain vary linearly with distance y from the neutral axis.
Radius of the circular arc into which the beam axis bends, in mm; strain at distance y is ε = y/R.
The product of Young's modulus E (N/mm²) and second moment of area I (mm⁴), in N·mm²; it is the beam's resistance to bending.
Distance in mm from the neutral axis to the farthest point of the section, where bending stress is largest.
Z = I/y_max, in mm³; the single number that converts allowable stress into moment capacity.
The maximum bending moment a section can carry safely, M = σ_allow × Z, in N·mm when σ is in N/mm² and Z in mm³.
m = E_stiffer/E_weaker, a pure number; stress in the stiffer material is m times the stress at the same distance in the weaker one.
An equivalent one-material section in which the width of the stiffer material is multiplied by m so that the whole section can be treated with one formula.
Q = A'ȳ', where A' is the area of the part of the section beyond the level considered (mm²) and ȳ' its centroid distance from the neutral axis (mm); Q is in mm³.
τ = VQ/(Ib), with V the shear force (N), Q in mm³, I in mm⁴ and b the width at that level (mm); τ comes out in N/mm².
q = VQ/I, in N/mm; it is the shear force transmitted per unit length along a joint or a flange-to-web connection.
The point in the cross-section through which a transverse load must pass so that the section bends without twisting.
A beam whose section is varied along the span so that the extreme fibre stress stays the same everywhere; it saves material.
The working stress obtained by dividing the yield or ultimate stress by a factor of safety; the design must keep σ_max ≤ σ_allow.

takeaways: The centroid fixes where the neutral axis sits, and the second moment of area about that axis fixes how stiff the section is in bending.
The bending equation M/I = σ/y = E/R packs three ideas into one line: moment capacity, stress at any depth, and how sharply the beam curves.
Bending stress is linear across the depth and zero at the neutral axis, so material near the centre of a section does very little work.
Section modulus Z = I/y_max is the practical design number: capacity M = σZ, and bigger Z for the same area means a more efficient shape.
In a flitched beam the two materials share the moment in proportion to their E values, so a transformed section with a modular ratio lets one formula handle both.
Shear stress does not stay uniform: it is zero at the top and bottom fibres, is maximum at the neutral axis for a rectangle, and is carried mostly by the web in an I-section.
Shear flow q = VQ/I tells you how much force must be carried by bolts or welds per millimetre of length.
A load applied away from the shear centre adds twisting to bending, so bolts and welds feel extra forces that plain bending formulas miss.
Design is a double check: Z must be large enough for the bending moment and the shear area large enough for the shear force.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always combine a derivation (bending equation or the shear stress formula) with a clearly labelled stress distribution diagram and a worked numerical check, so show assumptions, units and sketches, not just algebra.

bank.q: State the assumptions of the theory of simple bending and derive the equation M/I = σ/y = E/R. Explain what each symbol means and its unit.
outline: List assumptions: plane sections remain plane, material is homogeneous and elastic, E is the same in tension and compression, stresses stay within the proportional limit, the beam is initially straight.
Draw two sections a distance dx apart rotated relative to each other; strain at distance y is ε = y/R.
Apply Hooke's law: σ = E y/R.
Equate the internal moment of the stress force about the neutral axis to M and get M = EI/R.
Combine to write M/I = σ/y = E/R and define every symbol and unit.

bank.q: Define centroid and second moment of area. State the parallel axis theorem and explain why these two quantities decide where the neutral axis lies and how stiff a section is.
outline: Definition of centroid with the area formula; axis passes through the centroid.
Definition of I = Σa y², unit mm⁴.
Parallel axis theorem I = I_c + A d², with the meaning of each term.
The neutral axis coincides with the centroidal axis because the net axial force in pure bending is zero.
I about that axis gives flexural rigidity EI; a larger I means smaller curvature and smaller stress for the same moment.

bank.q: Explain section modulus. Derive Z for a rectangle and for a solid circle, and show why an I-section is more efficient than a rectangle of the same area.
outline: Z = I/y_max, unit mm³, capacity M = σZ.
Rectangle: I = bd³/12, y_max = d/2, Z = bd²/6.
Circle: I = πd⁴/64, y_max = d/2, Z = πd³/32.
I-section: most area is placed far from the neutral axis, so I and Z are large for the same area.
Rectangle of the same area puts a lot of material near the neutral axis where stress is low.

bank.q: What is a flitched beam? Explain the modular ratio and the transformed section method, and write the equations used to find the stresses in the two materials.
outline: Definition: two materials, typically timber and steel plates, bolted to act as one beam.
Assumptions: same curvature, no slip between the materials, strain is continuous at the interface.
Modular ratio m = E_steel/E_timber.
Transform steel into equivalent timber by multiplying its width by m; the section is then one material with I_eq.
σ_timber = M y/I_eq and σ_steel = m M y/I_eq.

bank.q: A T-section has flange 100 mm × 20 mm and web 20 mm × 120 mm. Find the centroid, the second moment of area about the centroidal axis, the section modulus, and the maximum bending stress for a bending moment of 15 kN·m.
outline: Split into two rectangles, take a reference edge, compute ȳ = Σa y/Σa correctly in mm.
Find I about the centroid with the parallel axis theorem for both rectangles; state the unit mm⁴.
Take y_max as the larger of the two distances to the top and bottom fibres.
Z = I/y_max in mm³.
σ_max = M/Z with M = 15 × 10⁶ N·mm, answer in N/mm².

bank.q: A simply supported beam of span 4 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m over its whole length. The section is rectangular, 150 mm wide, and the permissible bending stress is 10 N/mm². Find the required depth and then check the maximum shear stress.
outline: Maximum bending moment wL²/8 = 20 × 4²/8 = 40 kN·m.
Set M = σZ with σ = 10 N/mm² to get the required Z.
For a rectangle Z = bd²/6, solve for d in mm and round up to a practical size.
Maximum shear force V = wL/2 = 40 kN at the supports.
τ_max = 1.5 V/(bd) and compare with the permissible shear stress.

bank.q: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a shear force of 60 kN. Plot the shear stress distribution across the depth and find the shear stress at the neutral axis and at 50 mm from it.
outline: State τ = VQ/(Ib) and identify b = 100 mm constant for a rectangle.
At the neutral axis Q = b(d/2)(d/4) giving τ_max = 1.5 V/A.
At a general y, τ = 6V/(bd³) × (d²/4 − y²); substitute y = 50 mm.
Draw the parabola: zero at top and bottom fibres, maximum at the neutral axis.

bank.q: A timber beam 150 mm wide and 250 mm deep is strengthened by a steel plate 150 mm × 10 mm fixed to its top. Take E_steel = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm² and E_timber = 1 × 10⁴ N/mm². Find the moment the compound section can carry if the timber stress is limited to 8 N/mm².
outline: Modular ratio m = 2 × 10⁵/1 × 10⁴ = 20.
Transform steel into equivalent timber: width 150 × 20 = 3000 mm.
Locate the centroid of the transformed section, measuring from the bottom.
Compute I_eq about that centroid using parallel axis theorem for both parts.
σ_timber = M y_timber/I_eq gives M from the timber limit; check the steel stress as m times the timber stress at the same distance.

bank.q: Design a simply supported beam of span 6 m carrying a total factored load of 50 kN/m using an I-section. The permissible bending stress is 165 N/mm² and the permissible shear stress is 100 N/mm². Show the two checks.
outline: Maximum BM = wL²/8; maximum SF = wL/2, both with consistent units.
Required Z = M/σ_allow in mm³, then choose a standard I-section with Z at least this value.
Required shear area = V/τ_allow, then check that the web area (depth × web thickness) is adequate.
Note the maximum shear occurs at the supports where the bending moment is zero, and vice versa.
Comment on deflection serviceability as a third check in practice.

bank.q: Compare a rectangular section and an I-section of the same cross-sectional area for bending. Explain, using the stress distribution, why the I-section carries far more moment and where its weak point lies.
outline: Both have the same area, so the same weight per metre.
Bending stress grows linearly with y, so material near the neutral axis is lightly stressed and wasted.
Move that material to the flanges and I and Z rise sharply for the same area.
Sketch the linear stress diagram on both sections and mark the extreme fibres.
Weak point: the thin web carries most of the shear, so shear stress at the neutral axis becomes the limiting check.

bank.q: A load on a channel section is applied along the vertical centre line of the web. Explain why the section still twists, define the shear centre, and describe how you would locate it for a thin-walled channel.
outline: The shear flow in the flanges produces a horizontal force couple that is not balanced on the web centre line.
Twisting occurs unless the load passes through the shear centre.
Definition of shear centre: the point where the resultant of the internal shear forces acts, so a load there causes no twist.
For a singly symmetric section the shear centre lies on the axis of symmetry, but not at the centroid.
Method: take moments of the flange shear forces about the web, e ≈ (b²h²t)/(4I) type thin-walled result; state that bolts and welds must carry the added torsion.

bank.q: A beam has been checked in bending and found safe. Explain why it may still fail, using the shear stress distribution in an I-section, and state the design conditions for a beam that is safe in both flexure and shear.
outline: Bending stress is maximum at the extreme fibre but zero at the neutral axis.
Shear stress is maximum at the neutral axis where the bending stress is zero — the two maxima are at different depths.
In an I-section the web is thin, so τ = VQ/(Ib) can be high even when bending stress is low.
Design conditions: σ_max = M/Z ≤ σ_allow and τ_max = VQ/(Ib) ≤ τ_allow.
Also check shear flow at the flange-to-web junction, q = VQ/I per mm, for the weld or bolt size.

bank.q: Discuss when a flitched beam is preferred over a plain timber beam, and evaluate the effect of bolt slip and of a different coefficient of thermal expansion between the two materials.
outline: Timber alone needs a very deep section for large spans and moments; steel plates add stiffness cheaply.
The transformed section assumes no slip, so the bolts must be designed for the shear flow q = VQ/I at the interface.
Efficiency drops if the connection slips because plane sections no longer stay plane.
Different thermal expansion creates locked-in stresses even with no external load.
Verdict: efficient for strengthening and repair work when the connection is properly designed.

glossary.def: The geometric centre of an area, the point through which the neutral axis passes in pure bending.
The product of an area and the perpendicular distance of its centroid from an axis, measured in mm³.
The sum of area elements each multiplied by the square of its distance from an axis, measured in mm⁴; also called moment of inertia of the section.
The second moment of area about any axis equals that about a parallel centroidal axis plus the area times the square of the distance between them.
For a thin lamina, the polar second moment about an axis normal to the plane equals the sum of the two second moments about any two perpendicular axes in the plane.
Bending in which the shear force is zero throughout the length considered, so the bending moment is constant.
The line in a bent cross-section along which the longitudinal strain and stress are zero.
A cross-section that is flat before bending remains flat after bending, only rotating about the neutral axis.
The reciprocal of the radius of curvature, 1/R, in mm⁻¹; it equals M/(EI).
The product EI of a beam, in N·mm², which measures its resistance to bending.
The topmost or bottommost point of a section, that is, the point farthest from the neutral axis.
The second moment of area divided by the extreme fibre distance, I/y_max, in mm³.
The bending moment a section can safely resist, equal to the permissible stress times the section modulus.
The ratio of the Young's modulus of the stiffer material to that of the weaker material in a compound beam.
A fictitious one-material section, made by scaling one width by the modular ratio, that behaves the same way as the real compound section.
A beam made of two materials, commonly timber with steel plates, bolted or glued together to act as one.
The shear force transmitted per unit length along a longitudinal plane, equal to VQ/I and measured in N/mm.
The point in a section through which a transverse load must act if the beam is to bend without twisting.
The equal shear stress that acts on the longitudinal face at the same point as the transverse shear stress on the cross-section.
A beam whose cross-section changes along the span so that the extreme fibre stress remains constant.
The working stress a material is allowed to carry, obtained by dividing the yield or ultimate stress by a factor of safety.
The ratio of the failure stress of a material to the working stress chosen for design.
The maximum load a beam can support without exceeding the permissible bending or shear stress.
Choosing the depth-to-width ratio and the shape of a beam section so that material is used efficiently in bending.
